paper.title: Of Truth
paper.author: Francis Bacon
paper.edition: Complete 1625 essay; text transcribed from the 1884 collected edition. Editorial annotation numbers and running page numbers excluded.

rights: Public-domain original text and historical English edition. Source and edition records are kept outside the visible article.

blocks.en: What is truth? said jesting Pilate; and would not stay for an answer. Certainly, there be that delight in giddiness; and count it a bondage to fix a belief; affecting freewill in thinking as well as in acting. And though the sects of philosophers of that kind be gone, yet there remain certain discoursing wits which are of the same veins, though there be not so much blood in them as was in those of the ancients. But it is not only the difficulty and labor which men take in finding out of truth: nor again, that, when it is found, it imposeth upon men’s thoughts, that doth bring lies in favor; but a natural though corrupt love of the lie itself. One of the later schools of the Grecians examineth the matter, and is at a stand to think what should be in it that men should love lies; where neither they make for pleasure, as with poets; nor for advantage, as with the merchant, but for the lie’s sake. But I cannot tell; this same truth is a naked and open daylight, that doth not show the masks, and mummeries, and triumphs of the world, half so stately and daintily as candle-lights. Truth may perhaps come to the price of a pearl, that showeth best by day, but it will not rise to the price of a diamond or carbuncle, that showeth best in varied lights. A mixture of a lie doth ever add pleasure. Doth any man doubt, that if there were taken out of men’s minds vain opinions, flattering hopes, false valuations, imaginations as one would, and the like, but it would leave the minds of a number of men poor shrunken things, full of melancholy and indisposition, and unpleasing to themselves? One of the fathers, in great severity, called poesy “vinum dæmonum,” because it filleth the imagination, and yet it is but with the shadow of a lie. But it is not the lie that passeth through the mind, but the lie that sinketh in, and settleth in it, that doth the hurt, such as we spake of before. But howsoever these things are thus in men’s depraved judgments and affections, yet truth, which only doth judge itself, teacheth that the inquiry of truth, which is the love-making, or wooing of it, the knowledge of truth, which is the presence of it, and the belief of truth, which is the enjoying of it, is the sovereign good of human nature. The first creature of God, in the works of the days, was the light of the sense; the last was the light of reason; and his sabbath work, ever since, is the illumination of his Spirit. First, he breathed light upon the face of the matter, or chaos; then he breathed light into the face of man; and still he breatheth and inspireth light into the face of his chosen. The poet that beautified the sect, that was otherwise inferior to the rest, saith yet excellently well: “It is a pleasure to stand upon the shore, and to see ships tossed upon the sea; a pleasure to stand in the window of a castle, and to see a battle, and the adventures thereof below; but no pleasure is comparable to the standing upon the vantage-ground of truth” (a hill not to be commanded, and where the air is always clear and serene), “and to see the errors, and wanderings, and mists, and tempests, in the vale below;” so always that this prospect be with pity, and not with swelling or pride. Certainly it is heaven upon earth, to have a man’s mind move in charity, rest in providence, and turn upon the poles of truth.
blocks.zh: ‘真理是什么？’爱开玩笑的彼拉多问道，却不肯留下来等一个回答。确实，有些人喜欢思想飘忽不定，把固定一种信念看作束缚，既追求行动上的自由意志，也追求思考上的自由意志。这类哲学家的学派虽然已经消失，仍有一些爱议论的聪明人，与古人有同样的脾性，只是血气不如他们旺盛。谎言受到欢迎，不仅因为寻找真理的艰难和劳苦，也不仅因为真理一旦找到，就会约束人的思想，还因为人天然地——尽管这种倾向已经败坏——喜爱谎言本身。希腊后期某一学派曾研究这个问题，却想不明白：当谎言既不像诗人的谎言那样带来愉悦，也不像商人的谎言那样带来利益时，人为什么仍会为了谎言本身而喜爱它？我也说不清楚。真理就像裸露而明亮的白昼；在这种光线下，世间的面具、假扮和盛大表演，显得远不如烛光下那样壮丽悦目。真理的价值也许能比得上珍珠，珍珠在日光下最好看；但它不会升到钻石或红宝石的价值，因为后者在变幻的灯光下才最出色。掺入一点谎言，总会增加乐趣。有谁会怀疑，假如从人们心里拿走虚妄的见解、讨人喜欢的希望、错误的估价、顺着心愿的想象等等，许多人的心就会变成贫乏、萎缩的东西，充满忧郁和不安，连自己也不喜欢？一位教父曾严厉地把诗称作‘魔鬼之酒’，因为它灌满人的想象，尽管其中不过是谎言的影子。然而，造成伤害的，并不是从心中经过的谎言，而是沉入心里、留在其中的谎言，正如前面所说的那一种。无论败坏的判断和情感怎样使人如此，唯有真理能判断自身；它教导我们，探求真理，如同追求和求爱；认识真理，如同与它相会；相信真理，如同享有它——这三者是人性中至高的善。上帝在创世诸日里最先创造的是感官之光，最后创造的是理性之光；此后安息日的工作，则一直是以其精神照亮人。起初，他向物质或混沌的表面吹入光；随后，他向人的脸上吹入光；如今，他仍向自己选民的脸上吹入、注入光。有一位诗人，曾为一个本来不如其他学派的学派增光，却说出了极美的话：‘站在岸上，看海上的船只颠簸，是一种乐趣；站在城堡的窗口，看下面的战斗和种种遭遇，也是乐趣；但没有什么乐趣，比得上站在真理的制高点’——那是一座无法被别处俯视的高丘，空气永远澄明宁静——‘看山谷下面的错误、徘徊、迷雾和风暴’。但观看这一切时，应当怀着怜悯，而不是自满和骄傲。一个人的心若能行于仁爱、安于天意、围绕真理而运转，那确实就是人间的天堂。

blocks.en: To pass from theological and philosophical truth to the truth of civil business; it will be acknowledged, even by those that practise it not, that clear and round dealing is the honor of man’s nature, and that mixture of falsehood is like alloy in coin of gold and silver, which may make the metal work the better, but it embaseth it. For these winding and crooked courses are the goings of the serpent; which goeth basely upon the belly, and not upon the feet. There is no vice that doth so cover a man with shame, as to be found false and perfidious; and therefore Montaigne saith prettily, when he inquired the reason why the word of the lie should be such a disgrace, and such an odious charge: saith he, “If it be well weighed, to say that a man lieth, is as much as to say that he is brave towards God and a coward towards men. For a lie faces God, and shrinks from man;” surely, the wickedness of falsehood and breach of faith cannot possibly be so highly expressed, as in that it shall be the last peal to call the judgments of God upon the generations of men: it being foretold, that, when “Christ cometh,” he shall not “find faith upon the earth.”
blocks.zh: 从神学和哲学的真理，转到世俗事务中的真实，即使那些不肯践行的人也会承认，坦率而诚实地处事，是人性的光荣；掺入虚假，就像在金银钱币中掺入合金，虽然可能使金属更容易加工，却降低了它的成色。那些弯曲迂回的行径，正如蛇的爬行：它卑下地用肚腹贴地，而不用脚行走。没有哪一种恶习，能像被人发现虚假和背信那样，使人蒙上如此的羞耻。蒙田探究为什么说人撒谎，会是如此丢脸的事情、如此可憎的指控时，曾说得妙：‘仔细衡量，说一个人撒谎，无异于说他对上帝勇敢，对人却怯懦。因为谎言敢面对上帝，却在人面前退缩。’虚假与背信的邪恶，实在不可能有更强烈的表达了：它们将成为最后一阵钟声，召来上帝对人类历代的审判。因为预言说，当‘基督来临’时，他将在‘地上找不到信德’。
